qs.q: A 65-year-old heavy smoker presents with a central lung mass and signs of excessive antidiuretic hormone secretion leading to severe hyponatraemia. Biopsy of the central mass is most likely to reveal which of the following histological diagnoses?
qs.e: Small cell carcinoma is a central neuroendocrine lung tumour strongly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like SIADH. Adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma are typically peripheral lesions.

qs.q: Where are the neuronal cell bodies located that synthesize Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) prior to its storage in the posterior pituitary?
o: Arcuate nucleus, located in the mediobasal hypothalamus.
Paraventricular nucleus, synthesizes oxytocin and CRH.
Ventromedial nucleus, a hypothalamic satiety center.
Supraoptic nucleus, site of ADH synthesis.
qs.e: Antidiuretic hormone is primarily synthesized in the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus, while oxytocin is synthesized in the paraventricular nucleus. Both are transported down axons for posterior pituitary release.

qs.q: A child with pneumonia develops euvolaemic hyponatraemia due to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism of this disorder?
qs.e: SIADH involves unregulated release of ADH leading to impaired renal free water excretion and dilutional hyponatraemia. Primary sodium wasting conditions typically present with volume depletion rather than euvolaemia.

qs.q: An MDMA ('ecstasy') user is brought to the emergency department. Which electrolyte abnormality is uniquely associated with excessive water drinking and inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion in these patients?
qs.e: Ecstasy users may develop hyponatraemia as a result of excessive water drinking and inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion. The other electrolyte disturbances are not characteristic of MDMA-induced fluid imbalance.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as vasopressin, is a hormone that helps the body conserve water. It is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary gland. ADH primarily acts on the kidneys to increase water reabsorption.

sections.p: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is a crucial hormone for maintaining fluid balance in the body. It is produced in the hypothalamus and then transported to the posterior pituitary gland for storage and release. Its main function is to regulate water reabsorption by the kidneys, thereby controlling urine concentration and body water content.
b: Synthesized in the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
Stored and released from the posterior pituitary gland.
Primary role is water conservation.

sections.p: ADH acts primarily on the renal collecting ducts and distal convoluted tubules. It increases the permeability of these segments to water by promoting the insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane. This allows more water to be reabsorbed from the urine back into the bloodstream, leading to concentrated urine and conservation of body water.
b: Increases water permeability in renal collecting ducts and distal convoluted tubules.
Inserts aquaporin-2 channels into cell membranes.
Results in increased water reabsorption and concentrated urine.

sections.p: The release of ADH is tightly regulated by the body's hydration status. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in plasma osmolality, while baroreceptors detect changes in blood volume and pressure. These signals stimulate or inhibit ADH release to maintain homeostasis.
b: Increased plasma osmolality (hypernatremia) stimulates ADH release.
Decreased blood volume or pressure stimulates ADH release.
Alcohol and cold can inhibit ADH release.

sections.p: Dysregulation of ADH can lead to significant fluid imbalances. Both deficiency and excess of ADH have distinct clinical syndromes, impacting the body's ability to manage water. Understanding these conditions is vital for diagnosis and management.
b: Deficiency of ADH causes Central Diabetes Insipidus.
Excessive ADH secretion causes Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion (SIADH).

sections.p: ADH plays a critical role in several clinical conditions. Central Diabetes Insipidus results from insufficient ADH, leading to excessive urination and thirst. SIADH, on the other hand, involves excessive ADH, causing water retention and hyponatremia. Ectopic ADH production, often from small-cell lung cancer, is a significant cause of SIADH.
b: Central Diabetes Insipidus: Characterized by polyuria and polydipsia due to ADH deficiency.
SIADH: Characterized by hyponatremia and concentrated urine due to excessive ADH.
Small-cell lung cancer is a common cause of ectopic ADH production (paraneoplastic syndrome).

t.b: Answers: Is the patient's blood too concentrated or too dilute? High osmolality suggests dehydration or ADH deficiency; low osmolality suggests overhydration or SIADH.
Answers: How concentrated is the patient's urine? High urine osmolality with low serum osmolality suggests SIADH; low urine osmolality with high serum osmolality suggests Diabetes Insipidus.
Answers: Is there hyponatremia or hypernatremia? Hyponatremia is a hallmark of SIADH; hypernatremia is common in Diabetes Insipidus.

sections.p: When considering ADH, always think about its primary function: water conservation. Relate its regulation to plasma osmolality and blood volume. Remember the two main clinical syndromes associated with its dysfunction and their key differentiating features.
b: ADH is made in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary.
Its release is stimulated by hypernatremia and decreased blood volume.
It increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, not the ascending loop of Henle.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of extreme thirst and excessive urination (polyuria and polydipsia)
Confusion, seizures, or altered mental status (can indicate severe hyponatremia or hypernatremia)
Significant swelling (edema) or rapid weight gain/loss

faq.q: What is the primary function of ADH?
faq.a: The primary function of ADH is to increase water reabsorption in the kidneys, helping the body conserve water and concentrate urine.

faq.q: Where is ADH produced and released?
faq.a: ADH is produced in the hypothalamus and then stored and released from the posterior pituitary gland.

faq.q: What conditions are caused by too much or too little ADH?
faq.a: Too little ADH causes Central Diabetes Insipidus, while too much ADH causes Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH).
